chapters.title: Chapter 6: When to Hedge and When Not To

lessons.title: Event-Based Hedging: Budget, Elections, Results, and RBI Policy

children.text: If permanent hedging is too expensive, the obvious compromise is to hedge only around dates that matter: the Budget on 1 February, RBI policy days, results season, election counting day. This sounds disciplined, and for one or two genuinely large events it is. The trap is that India's calendar is crowded, and an investor who hedges every scheduled event has quietly rebuilt a permanent hedge with extra brokerage. This lesson gives you a way to tell the events worth protecting against from the ones that only feel dangerous, and a method for reading what the market has already priced in.

body.text: Options already contain the market's forecast of an event. You are not buying protection against the event, you are betting the move will be bigger than the price implies. Hedge an event only when a bigger-than-expected move would genuinely break a goal.

children.text: India's Event Calendar

body.title: The recurring dates that make investors nervous

events.title: Union Budget
events.description: Tax and spending announcements. Index moves on Budget day are usually modest, though changes to capital gains or transaction taxes can cause sharper reactions.

events.title: RBI monetary policy
events.description: Rate and stance decisions, roughly every two months. Index moves are typically small, but banking and rate-sensitive stocks can move more.

events.title: Quarterly results season
events.description: Individual stocks can move sharply on results day. The index itself usually absorbs them, since not all companies report together.

events.title: US Federal Reserve decisions
events.description: Global rate expectations move foreign flows into and out of Indian equities, sometimes with a delayed effect here.

events.date: Every five years, plus state polls
events.title: General and state elections
events.description: The one recurring event that has repeatedly produced very large single-day index moves, as 4 June 2024 showed.

events.title: Shocks with no date
events.description: Wars, pandemics, global credit events and tariff announcements. Precisely the events you cannot hedge in advance, because nobody publishes their calendar.

body.text: Read that last row again. The events that caused the two deepest Indian drawdowns in living memory, the 2008 credit crisis and the 2020 pandemic, were not on anybody's calendar. Event hedging is, by construction, protection against the risks you can see coming. It is no help at all against the ones that actually do the most damage, which is an argument for cheap standing catastrophe cover rather than a series of event hedges.

children.text: What the Market Has Already Priced In

markDefs.definition: Buying both a call and a put at the same strike and expiry. Its combined price is a rough measure of the move the market expects by that expiry, in either direction.

children.text: Before you hedge an event, find out what the market thinks it is worth. The quickest gauge is the price of the at-the-money
straddle
for the expiry that covers the event. Add the at-the-money call and put premiums together and divide by the index level. That percentage is roughly the move the market is pricing in.

body.latex: \text{Implied move} \approx \frac{\text{ATM call premium} + \text{ATM put premium}}{\text{Index level}}
body.caption: A rough but useful reading. If the Nifty is at 25,000 and the ATM call and put together cost ₹625, the market is pricing a move of about 2.5% by that expiry.

body.title: Read the implied move
body.prompt: The Nifty is at 25,000. For the expiry just after the Budget, the 25,000 call trades at ₹320 and the 25,000 put at ₹300. What move is the market implying, as a percentage? (Two decimal places.)
body.explanation: (320 + 300) ÷ 25,000 = 0.0248, or about 2.48%. If your tolerable drawdown is 8%, an event the market expects to move the index about 2.5% is very unlikely to break your goal, and paying for protection against it is hard to justify.

children.text: Four Tests Before Hedging Any Event
Size: could it break a goal?
Compare the implied move with your tolerable drawdown. If the event would have to be several times worse than expected to matter, skip it.
Timing: is the money needed soon?
A fall you have five years to recover from is not the same as one that arrives two months before you need the money.
Price: is protection still cheap?
Check India VIX. If it has already doubled in anticipation, as it did before the 2024 election results, you are buying at the worst time.
Behaviour: what will you do without it?
If the honest answer is that you would panic sell on a bad headline, a modest hedge may be cheaper than that mistake.

body.caption: A rough guide to which events pass the tests

cells: Rarely. Consider it only for a concentrated banking or rate-sensitive portfolio
Usually modest, occasionally sharp on tax changes
Only if a near-term goal leaves you no room at all
Small at index level, large for single stocks
Not for an index portfolio. Sometimes for a concentrated stock holding
Has produced very large single-day moves
Often yes, if you have a near-term goal, and only if bought well in advance
US Fed decisions and global shocks
Rarely worth a specific hedge, because the transmission is unpredictable
Cannot be hedged in advance. This is what cheap standing cover is for

body.title: Which event earns a hedge?
body.question: Sudha has ₹60 lakh in Nifty index funds and needs ₹50 lakh in four months for a property payment. Four events fall inside that window. Which one most justifies a hedge?
options: An RBI policy meeting, where the market implies a 0.6% move
Quarterly results season, spread over several weeks
A general election result day, where the market implies a 4.5% move
A US Fed meeting, where Indian markets have historically reacted modestly
body.explanation: Her tolerable drawdown is 1 − 50 ÷ 60, about 16.7%. Only the election result has a record of producing moves large enough to approach that, and on 4 June 2024 the Nifty fell 5.93% in a single session after an implied move of similar size. The other three are unlikely to threaten her goal.

children.text: Buy Early, Not on the Eve

body.title: Timing the purchase of an event hedge

columns.label: Bought four to eight weeks early
points: Implied volatility is usually still low, so the premium is a fraction of the later price
You gain if volatility rises into the event, as well as if the market falls
You pay for time you may not need
Requires planning rather than reacting to headlines

columns.label: Bought in the final days
points: Implied volatility is at its peak, so the same strike costs far more
Volatility crush after the event drains value fast, even if you were right about direction
Shorter exposure, so less time decay in absolute terms
Feels safest, which is exactly why it is crowded and expensive

stats.context: Weeks before the election result, protection was near its cheapest

stats.label: India VIX, 31 May 2024
stats.context: Just before exit polls, the same cover cost several times more

stats.label: Nifty, 4 June 2024
stats.context: The event itself, followed by a record close three sessions later

body.text: There is a second trap on the other side of the event. Once the result is known, implied volatility collapses. A put bought at high volatility can lose money even if the market falls, simply because the fall was smaller than the price implied. Event hedges should be sized and timed on the assumption that you will not be paid for being roughly right, only for being very right.

body.title: After the announcement
body.textWithBlank: The sharp fall in implied volatility immediately after an event is resolved is called a volatility ___.
body.explanation: It is the reason event hedges must be bought early and judged on the whole portfolio. After the event, the option loses value from both time decay and the drop in implied volatility.

body.title: The investor who hedges everything
body.scenario: Mohit, 46, a project manager in Noida, has ₹40 lakh in index funds and a 15-year horizon. After reading about event risk, he decides to buy a two-week Nifty put before every major event: the Budget, each of the six RBI policy meetings, and each of the four results seasons. Each hedge costs him about 0.4% of his portfolio. He is pleased with how systematic this feels.
body.prompt: What is Mohit actually doing, and what would you suggest instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Count the events: 1 Budget + 6 RBI meetings + 4 results seasons = 11 hedges a year, at about 0.4% each. That is roughly 4.4% of his portfolio annually, about ₹1.76 lakh on ₹40 lakh.
2. That is the same cost as the permanent near-money hedging that Lesson 1 of this chapter showed to be so damaging, but with worse coverage, because he is unprotected between events.
3. Most of these events do not threaten him. The implied move before an RBI policy is usually well under 1%, and he has no near-term goal at all, so even a 10% fall would not break anything.
4. He is also exposed precisely where event hedging fails: the unscheduled shock that arrives in a quiet week when he holds no puts.
5. Better approaches: no hedge at all, given his horizon; or, if he wants to sleep at night, one cheap far out-of-the-money put rolled quarterly at well under 1% a year, which covers the calendar and the surprises alike.
The lesson: hedging every event is permanent hedging with extra transaction costs and gaps in cover. Pick the one or two events that could actually break a goal, and ignore the rest.

body.title: Reading event expectations off the option chain

children.text: Two quick checks tell you how seriously the market is taking an event:
Compare expiries. Look at the implied volatility of the expiry just before the event and the one just after. A large jump between them is the market pricing the event itself.
Compare the straddle with history. If the implied move for a Budget is 2.5% and past Budget days have typically moved the index around 1%, protection is expensive relative to what usually happens.
Neither check tells you what will happen. They tell you what you are being charged, which is the only part of the transaction you control.

body.title: An event hedging protocol
steps: At the start of the year, list only the events that fall inside a window where you have a real goal.
For each, calculate the implied move from the at-the-money straddle for the expiry covering the event.
Compare that implied move with your tolerable drawdown, and drop any event that cannot realistically threaten it.
For events that survive, buy protection four to eight weeks ahead while India VIX is still low, using an expiry that ends after the event.
Decide in advance what you will do with the hedge immediately after the event: close it, keep it, or roll it.

body.label: NSE Option Chain
body.description: Add the at-the-money call and put premiums for the expiry covering an event to read the market's implied move before deciding whether to hedge.

cards.definition: A scheduled date that could move the market sharply, such as election results or the Budget.
Roughly the at-the-money call plus put premium divided by the index level. What the market expects by that expiry.
The extra implied volatility built into options covering an event date.
The collapse in implied volatility once an event is resolved, which drains option value quickly.
Hedging only scheduled events, leaving you unprotected against the unscheduled shocks that cause the deepest falls.

points: Options already price in scheduled events. Hedging one is a bet that the move will be larger than the market expects.
Read the implied move from the at-the-money straddle and compare it with your tolerable drawdown before paying for protection.
Most recurring Indian events, including RBI policy and results season, rarely threaten a diversified portfolio. Election results have.
Buy event protection four to eight weeks early while India VIX is low, never on the eve when volatility has already doubled.
Expect a volatility crush after the event: being roughly right about direction may still lose money.
Hedging every event costs as much as permanent hedging and leaves gaps. The deepest crashes were never on the calendar.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Descriptions of typical event impacts are general observations, not statistical findings, and past behaviour around any event does not predict future behaviour. Option premiums used are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before hedging around any event.
